points.text: Your partition key is the minute window, so every user's counter for a minute lives on one partition and the per-user lookup depends on the secondary index rather than the primary access path. A key built around the user (with the window alongside) would fit how checks actually read and write far better.

Partitioning by message_id scatters every message of a chat across nodes, so opening a chat cannot use locality: it depends on the secondary index on chat_id to gather rows, and recent messages of one chat sit nowhere together. Partitioning by chat_id with message ordering inside the partition fits how this is written and read.

The partition key is region, so every feed in a region lands on the same partition and a feed open must find its row through a secondary lookup instead of the key. The feed is read and written per user, so the key should follow the user, not the region.
points.quote: table kv.feeds(region pk, user_id, posts, updated_at) index(user_id)

points.text: A post must fan out into the feeds of everyone who follows the author, but the write path writes once and ends. There is no queue or worker stage, so follower feeds are never rebuilt and the promise that a post updates the feeds it belongs to cannot be met.
points.quote: write POST:     client > lb > api > ids > kv then invalidate cache

points.text: The single invalidation after the write can only clear the one feed key involved in this request, while the post lands inside many followers' cached feeds. As written, those cached copies are not reached by this invalidation, so the cache fights the fanout the post needs.

created_at is the primary key, so two links created at the same moment share a key and one row overwrites the other; links get lost. The reads go by code anyway, so created_at is the wrong thing to key on.

player_id as the primary key allows only one row per player, but scores are tracked per game. A player joining a new game would overwrite the row for an earlier one, or at best force a choice between games. The key needs to scope a player to a game.
points.quote: table db.scores(player_id pk, game_id, score, rank) index(game_id)

points.text: Storing rank as a column means every score change can shift the rank of many other players, and the stored values go stale unless all of them are rewritten on each submit. The top list should derive order from score rather than trust a saved rank.

With seat_id as the primary key alone, the same seat cannot exist as a separate row per show, so the design cannot represent the same physical seat across different shows (or the final's multiple shows). The key needs to capture both the show and the seat so each show's seat is its own row.

You are keeping the photo bytes themselves in the nosql store. Key-value stores are meant for small records, not tens of terabytes of binary blobs; this is what the object store part exists for. Serve the bytes from there behind the CDN, keeping only small lookup records elsewhere.

The table stores a chat's messages but has nothing that records when each message was sent or its order within the chat. Opening a chat must return its recent messages, which cannot be identified or ordered from these columns alone.

Random ids never repeat, which satisfies the uniqueness rule, but they carry no time ordering, so they cannot serve as a stand-in sort key for messages either. An ordered id or a stored timestamp would make 'recent messages' well defined.

A one-second lifetime on the CDN means nearly every view falls through to your origin instead of being served at the edge, even though a photo never changes once uploaded. That works against the CDN's whole purpose for this read-heavy, few-hot-photos workload; the lifetime can be much longer because names never repeat.

The table keeps messages under a chat partition, but nothing indicates how recent messages are returned in order within that partition. Opening a chat promises its recent messages; your snowflake message ids carry time order, so make sure the read path actually sorts or clusters by that rather than returning partition order.

points.quote: write BOOK:      client > lb > api ~> queue > worker > ids > db then invalidate cache

points.text: Because the reply goes out before the worker checks and claims the seat, a fan is told they booked before anyone knows the seat was free. A lost or failed job leaves them with a phantom confirmation and no way to know it failed.

You route the check through a queue, so the actual count happens later, after the client has already been told yes. The check promises to count the call and answer whether the user is over the limit, but by the time the worker runs, the answer has no bearing on this call. The decision itself has to happen in the request path, against the store, at check time.

Your counters table keys only on the user, so the time window lives inside the row. That means every window change depends on correctly reading, comparing and resetting that row, and an out-of-date write could carry the previous window forward. A key that captures the user and the current window fits this naturally and keeps the past minute from leaking into the next.

Your partition key is the window, so every user's counter for the minute lands in one partition and the key alone does not identify a user's row; both the check and the usage read actually want a user-scoped key (with the window as part of it or a sort key). Worth reconsidering how a given user's counter is located.

You may want the key to reflect both the game and the player.
